46 terms

The words on the paperwork

Every term you are likely to meet at a registry counter, a bank or a licence inspection, with the characters, the pinyin, and what it actually decides.

Company formation in China is discussed in a vocabulary that carries legal weight and is almost never translated in the room. Knowing the characters on a business licence is the difference between understanding what you own and being told what you own.

The pinyin is included because you will hear these words spoken long before you see them written. Say the term out loud once; it is the fastest way to stop a conversation that has moved past you.

ABCDEFGHILNOPRSTUVW

A

  • 年度审计

    Niándù shěnjì

    Annual audit

    The audit of the annual financial statements that most foreign-invested companies must complete and file. Dividends, capital reductions and many bank transactions depend on having the audit report in hand.

    Where this matters: The annual compliance calendarGetting money out of China

  • 年度报告

    Niándù bàogào

    Annual report

    The yearly filing to the market regulator, due between 1 January and 30 June. Missing it puts the company on the abnormal-operations list, which freezes bank activity and bidding.

    Where this matters: The annual compliance calendar

  • 公司章程

    Gōngsī zhāngchéng

    Articles of association

    The constitutional document filed with the registry. It governs board composition, voting, profit distribution and transfer of shares; a bad set of articles is expensive to fix later.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicleDo you need a Hong Kong holding company?

B

  • 营业执照

    Yíngyè zhízhào

    Business licence

    The document that proves a company exists. It carries the company name, legal representative, registered capital, business scope and registered address, and every bank, landlord and licence application will ask for it.

    Where this matters: The registered address, and why the cheap one costs moreWFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicle

  • 经营范围

    Jīngyíng fànwéi

    Business scope

    The list of activities a company is registered to carry out, printed on the licence. Anything requiring a licence must be tied to one, and invoicing outside the scope is a common audit finding.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicleFapiao for foreign founders

C

  • 资本金账户

    Zīběnjīn zhànghù

    Capital account

    The account through which foreign shareholders inject registered capital. Money entering it is registered with the foreign-exchange authority and can later be used for permitted purposes or repatriated.

    Where this matters: Opening a corporate bank accountGetting money out of China

  • 公章

    Gōngzhāng

    Company seal (chop)

    The red stamp that legally executes documents on behalf of the company. Physical control of the seal is control of the company, which is why it matters in shareholder disputes.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicleClosing a company in China

  • 对公账户

    Duìgōng zhànghù

    Corporate bank account

    A bank account in the company's name, opened in person after registration. Without it the company cannot receive capital, pay salaries or invoice, and opening one is often the slowest step in the whole setup.

    Where this matters: Opening a corporate bank accountThe registered address, and why the cheap one costs more

  • 企业所得税

    Qǐyè suǒdéshuì

    Corporate income tax (CIT)

    Tax on company profits at a standard 25%. Small low-profit companies can qualify for an effective 5% rate, and high-tech enterprises for 15%, but both require meeting conditions and filing for them.

    Where this matters: Getting money out of ChinaThe annual compliance calendar

  • 报关单位备案

    Bàoguān dānwèi bèi'àn

    Customs declarant registration

    The free filing that lets a company declare its own imports and exports through the single-window system. Without it, goods must be cleared through an agent, and the company cannot recover import VAT as a general taxpayer.

    Where this matters: Importing goods into China

  • 海关登记

    Hǎiguān dēngjì

    Customs registration

    The registration that lets a company import or export in its own name. It is separate from the business licence and requires the company to have its foreign-trade operator status recorded.

    Where this matters: The negative list, plainly

D

  • 注销

    Zhùxiāo

    Deregistration

    The final cancellation of the company's registration, after liquidation and tax clearance. Until it is done, the company remains alive for filings, penalties and the legal representative's record.

    Where this matters: Closing a company in China

E

  • 股权转让

    Gǔquán zhuǎnràng

    Equity transfer

    The sale of shares to an existing or new shareholder. It requires written notice to the other shareholders, who have 30 days to exercise a right of first refusal, plus tax on the gain and a registration change within 30 days.

    Where this matters: Changing shareholders and closing the companyDo you need a Hong Kong holding company?

F

  • 外商投资准入负面清单

    Wàishāng tóuzī zhǔnrù fùmiàn qīngdān

    Foreign investment negative list

    The national catalogue of sectors where foreign investment is prohibited or restricted. Anything not on the list is open, but a sector licence may still apply.

    Where this matters: The negative list, plainlyDo you need a China entity at all?

  • 外汇登记

    Wàihuì dēngjì

    Foreign-exchange registration

    The filing that links a company to its foreign shareholder for currency purposes. It is usually handled by the bank at account opening, and without it capital cannot be injected or profits remitted.

    Where this matters: Opening a corporate bank accountGetting money out of China

  • 外商投资企业

    Wàishāng tóuzī qǐyè

    Foreign-invested enterprise (FIE)

    The collective legal category for companies with foreign investment, governed since 2020 by the Foreign Investment Law. A WFOE and a JV are both FIEs.

    Where this matters: The negative list, plainlyWFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicle

  • 自由贸易试验区

    Zìyóu màoyì shìyànqū

    Free-trade zone (FTZ)

    A designated area with a shorter negative list and pilot rules on foreign exchange, customs and investment. Shanghai, Shenzhen, Guangzhou and others have one; benefits are real but zone-specific.

    Where this matters: The negative list, plainlyDo you need a Hong Kong holding company?

G

  • 一般纳税人

    Yībān nàshuìrén

    General VAT taxpayer

    VAT status that allows input-VAT credit and the issuance of higher-rate fapiao. Most companies selling to other businesses need it; the registration is not automatic.

    Where this matters: Fapiao for foreign founders

H

  • 高新技术企业

    Gāoxīn jìshù qǐyè

    High-tech enterprise (HNTE)

    A certification that cuts corporate income tax to 15% and unlocks subsidies. It requires owned intellectual property, a qualifying R&D ratio and a local application process.

    Where this matters: Getting money out of China

  • 住房公积金

    Zhùfáng gōngjījīn

    Housing provident fund

    A compulsory savings contribution for employees, shared by employer and employee, used for housing. Foreign employees' participation varies by city and is often optional.

    Where this matters: Hiring your first employee in China

I

  • 个人所得税

    Gèrén suǒdéshuì

    Individual income tax (IIT)

    Tax on salaries and other personal income, withheld monthly by the employer. Foreign employees may qualify for special deductions, but the allowance rules are narrower than they were before 2022.

    Where this matters: Hiring your first employee in ChinaWork permits for foreign founders

L

  • 法定代表人

    Fǎdìng dàibiǎorén

    Legal representative

    The person who binds the company in law and appears on the licence. The role carries personal exposure for compliance failures, and a foreign legal representative must usually hold a work permit.

    Where this matters: Work permits for foreign foundersClosing a company in China

  • 清算

    Qīngsuàn

    Liquidation

    The process of winding up a company's affairs — creditors, tax, employees, assets — before deregistration. It is the long part of closing a Chinese company and cannot be skipped.

    Where this matters: Closing a company in China

N

  • 代持

    Dàichí

    Nominee shareholding

    Holding shares through a Chinese individual who appears on the register. Common because it is fast, risky because the nominee is legally the owner, and difficult to enforce without a written trust agreement.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicleDo you need a China entity at all?

O

  • 发票

    Fāpiào

    Official tax invoice (fapiao)

    The invoice issued through the tax authority's system. Chinese companies generally cannot deduct an expense without one, so the fapiao system shapes who you can buy from and how you get paid.

    Where this matters: Fapiao for foreign foundersGetting money out of China

P

  • 实缴资本

    Shíjiǎo zīběn

    Paid-in capital

    Capital that has actually been transferred into the company's capital account and verified. Banks and regulators look at paid-in, not subscribed, when judging whether the company can meet its obligations.

    Where this matters: Registered capital and the five-year ruleOpening a corporate bank account

R

  • 注册地址

    Zhùcè dìzhǐ

    Registered address

    The address on the business licence where the company is deemed to reside. It must be a real, documented space; a virtual or shared address can pass registration and still fail bank due diligence or an inspection.

    Where this matters: The registered address, and why the cheap one costs moreOpening a corporate bank account

  • 注册资本

    Zhùcè zīběn

    Registered capital

    The amount of capital the shareholders commit to contribute, written on the business licence. Since 2024 it must be paid in within five years, and it is the number creditors and regulators treat as the company's promise.

    Where this matters: Registered capital and the five-year ruleGetting money out of China

  • 外国企业常驻代表机构

    Wàiguó qǐyè chángzhù dàibiǎo jīgòu

    Representative office (RO)

    A non-trading liaison office of a foreign company. It may make contacts, do market research and coordinate, but it cannot sign contracts, invoice or receive business revenue in its own name.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicleDo you need a China entity at all?

  • 居留许可

    Jūliú xǔkě

    Residence permit

    The visa-equivalent that lets a foreign national stay in China for work, study or family reasons. A work permit is the prerequisite for a work-type residence permit.

    Where this matters: Work permits for foreign founders

S

  • 中外合资经营企业

    Zhōngwài hézī jīngyíng qǐyè

    Sino-foreign equity joint venture (JV)

    A company owned jointly by a foreign investor and a Chinese partner, with ownership, board seats and profit sharing set in the joint-venture contract and articles.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicleThe negative list, plainly

  • 小规模纳税人

    Xiǎoguīmó nàshuìrén

    Small-scale VAT taxpayer

    The default VAT status for small companies: a low rate (currently 1% on many services) and no input-VAT credit. Simple, but it can block you from selling to larger companies that need a 6% or 13% fapiao.

    Where this matters: Fapiao for foreign founders

  • 社会保险

    Shèhuì bǎoxiǎn

    Social insurance

    Mandatory pension, medical, unemployment, injury and maternity contributions for employees. Rates vary by city, and the employer share is a real addition to salary cost.

    Where this matters: Hiring your first employee in ChinaWork permits for foreign founders

  • 印花税

    Yìnhuāshuì

    Stamp duty

    A small transaction tax on specified documents, charged to both parties in most cases: 0.03% on sales contracts, 0.1% on leases, 0.05% on equity transfers and 0.025% on capital account books. It is easy to overlook and easy to accrue penalties on.

    Where this matters: The taxes a small China company actually paysOffice leases and registered premisesChanging shareholders and closing the company

  • 法定公积金

    Fǎdìng gōngjījīn

    Statutory reserve fund

    A fund built from 10% of after-tax profit until it reaches 50% of registered capital. Dividends cannot be distributed until the reserve is funded, which is one reason a profitable company can still be unable to pay out in its first years.

    Where this matters: Getting money out of ChinaThe taxes a small China company actually pays

  • 认缴资本

    Rènjiǎo zīběn

    Subscribed capital

    The capital a shareholder has promised to pay, as opposed to what has actually arrived. Under the five-year rule the gap between the two is a dated obligation, not an option.

    Where this matters: Registered capital and the five-year rule

  • 监事

    Jiānshì

    Supervisor

    A statutory oversight role required in a Chinese limited company, separate from the directors. It cannot be held by the legal representative or a director, which is why founders often appoint a colleague.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicle

T

  • 税务备案

    Shuìwù bèi'àn

    Tax recordal for outbound payments

    The filing that must be completed before a bank remits certain payments abroad — service fees, royalties, interest and similar current-account items above USD 50,000. The bank checks the recordal, the contract and the invoice before releasing the money.

    Where this matters: The capital account and foreign exchangeGetting money out of China

  • 税收协定

    Shuìshōu xiédìng

    Tax treaty

    A bilateral agreement that can reduce withholding tax on dividends, interest and royalties. China has treaties with most countries, but the rate applies only if the recipient qualifies and files for it.

    Where this matters: Getting money out of ChinaDo you need a Hong Kong holding company?

  • 商标

    Shāngbiāo

    Trademark

    A registered mark that gives exclusive rights in specified classes. China is first-to-file: the registration, not the use, creates the right, so a brand launched without filing can be lost to whoever files first.

    Where this matters: Trademarks and IP in ChinaCompany name and business scope

U

  • 统一社会信用代码

    Tǒngyī shèhuì xìnyòng dàimǎ

    Unified social credit code

    The 18-character identifier printed on the business licence. It is the company's tax number, customs number and filing key all at once.

    Where this matters: The annual compliance calendarOpening a corporate bank account

V

  • 增值税

    Zēngzhíshuì

    Value-added tax (VAT)

    The main indirect tax, charged on sales and reclaimed on purchases. The rate depends on the activity — 13% for goods, 9% for some services and transport, 6% for most modern services.

    Where this matters: Fapiao for foreign foundersGetting money out of China

  • 协议控制

    Xiéyì kòngzhì

    Variable interest entity (VIE)

    A structure where an offshore company controls a domestic operating company through contracts rather than shares, used where foreign ownership is restricted. It is a workaround with real enforcement risk, not a licence.

    Where this matters: The negative list, plainlyDo you need a Hong Kong holding company?

W

  • 外商独资企业

    Wàishāng dúzī qǐyè

    Wholly foreign-owned enterprise (WFOE)

    A limited liability company in China owned entirely by a foreign investor, with no Chinese shareholder. It can trade, hire, invoice and hold licences in its own name, which is why it is the default vehicle for a foreign founder.

    Where this matters: WFOE, JV or RO: choosing the vehicleDo you need a China entity at all?Do you need a Hong Kong holding company?

  • 代扣代缴

    Dàikòu dàijiǎo

    Withholding tax

    Tax withheld at source, most visibly the 10% on dividends paid to a foreign shareholder. A tax treaty can reduce the rate, but the reduced rate must be claimed with the right forms.

    Where this matters: Getting money out of ChinaDo you need a Hong Kong holding company?

  • 外国人工作许可证

    Wàiguórén gōngzuò xǔkězhèng

    Work permit for foreigners

    The permit that allows a foreign national to work for a specific employer. It is graded A, B and C; most founders qualify under B, which requires a degree, two years of experience and a salary above the local threshold.

    Where this matters: Work permits for foreign foundersHiring your first employee in China

If a term you met is missing, that is a gap worth reporting — tell us and it will be added with the same treatment.
